steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting RoDia, a new speech dataset for Romanian dialect identification. Cover the state of spoken dialect identification, why low-resource languages like Romanian need speech resources, and how RoDia differs from existing Romanian datasets.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Spoken dialect identification and its focus on widely spoken languages
- Romanian as a low-resource language with rich dialectal variation; VarDial
- Deep learning and the need for resources; text vs. speech datasets
- RoDia compared with existing Romanian text datasets
- Romanian audio datasets and what RoDia adds

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Spoken dialect identification
  - challenging task: fine-grained distinction between varieties of a language; similar implications to spoken language identification
  - more delicate, but less attention; mostly widely spoken languages: English, Chinese, Arabic
  - low-resource languages (Swiss German, Finnish) relatively underexplored
- Romanian
  - our focus: spoken dialect identification in Romanian, low-resource, intricate dialectal variation within Romania
  - Romance language, Latin roots; landscape shaped by historical, geographical, sociocultural factors
  - still low-resource, few studies on regional linguistic diversity
  - not unique: many languages with lower visibility on the global linguistic stage
  - VarDial workshop: main driver of interest in language variety / dialect identification, multiple shared tasks each year
- Resources
  - deep learning successful in speech processing -> used for low-resource languages -> growing need for resources
  - two kinds of dialect identification datasets: text-based and speech-based
  - text: written materials capturing variation, but may miss phonetic and prosodic characteristics key to dialect differentiation
  - audio datasets: more holistic, lexical disparities plus subtle intonations and accents
- RoDia vs. Romanian text datasets
  - first dataset for spoken dialect identification in Romania, in line with historical, geographical, sociocultural factors (to our knowledge)
  - MOROCO and MOROCO-Tweets: text, only two dialects: Romanian (= Muntenesc) and Moldavian (Moldovenesc)
  - RoDia: speech, five dialects (Figure 1)
  - extra dialects Ardelenesc, Bănăţean, Oltenesc: phonetic differences captured only in speech -> why MOROCO / MOROCO-Tweets only cover the other two
- Romanian audio datasets
  - few audio datasets in Romanian -> confirms low-resource
  - existing ones mainly for automatic speech recognition, ignore dialect diversity
  - RoDia: five dialects: Muntenesc (accepted as official language of Romania), Ardelenesc, Moldovenesc, Oltenesc, Bănăţean

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Spoken dialect identification has emerged as a challenging task that aims at a fine-grained distinction between the varieties of a certain language, and it has similar implications to spoken language identification. Even though it is a more delicate task, spoken dialect identification has received less attention, and most of it went to dialect identification for widely spoken languages such as English, Chinese and Arabic. Spoken dialect identification for low-resource languages, such as Swiss German and Finnish, has stayed relatively underexplored. Unlike prior studies, we focus on spoken language identification in Romanian, which is a low-resource language with intricate dialectal variations within the country of Romania. Romanian is a Romance language with Latin roots, and it has a rich linguistic landscape that was shaped by historical, geographical and sociocultural factors. But despite this linguistic complexity, Romanian is still a low-resource language, and there are only limited studies dedicated to understanding its regional linguistic diversity. This lack of resources is not unique to Romanian, and many other languages around the world have similar challenges because they have lower visibility on the global linguistic stage. The VarDial workshop is one of the main drivers of the growing interest in language variety and dialect identification, by organizing multiple shared tasks each year.

Because deep learning frameworks have been successful in speech processing, researchers started to use such methods for low-resource languages. This has led to a growing need for resources on low-resource languages. If we look at dialect identification datasets across different languages, we can distinguish two types of resources: text-based datasets and speech-based datasets. Various languages have benefited from text-based resources that use written materials capturing linguistic variations, but the auditory dimension of dialects adds an intricate layer of complexity. Text data is valuable, but it might not fully capture the nuanced phonetic and prosodic characteristics that are pivotal for telling dialects apart. Audio datasets, in contrast to text datasets, give a more holistic representation, and they capture not only the lexical disparities but also the subtle intonations and accents that are inherent in speech.

- RoDia vs. Romanian text datasets
  - to our knowledge first dataset for spoken dialect identification in Romania (historical, geographical, sociocultural factors)
  - MOROCO, MOROCO-Tweets: text, only Romanian (= Muntenesc) and Moldavian (Moldovenesc)
  - RoDia: speech, five dialects (Figure 1)
  - Ardelenesc, Bănăţean, Oltenesc: phonetic differences only in speech -> why the text datasets only have the other two
- Romanian audio datasets
  - few exist -> low-resource; mostly automatic speech recognition, ignore dialects
  - RoDia: Muntenesc (accepted as official language of Romania), Ardelenesc, Moldovenesc, Oltenesc, Bănăţean

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Spoken dialect identification has emerged as a challenging task that aims at a fine-grained distinction between the varieties of a certain language, and it has similar implications to spoken language identification. Even though it is a more delicate task, spoken dialect identification has received less attention, and most of it went to dialect identification for widely spoken languages such as English, Chinese and Arabic. Spoken dialect identification for low-resource languages, such as Swiss German and Finnish, has stayed relatively underexplored. Unlike prior studies, we focus on spoken language identification in Romanian, which is a low-resource language with intricate dialectal variations within the country of Romania. Romanian is a Romance language with Latin roots, and it has a rich linguistic landscape that was shaped by historical, geographical and sociocultural factors. But despite this linguistic complexity, Romanian is still a low-resource language, and there are only limited studies dedicated to understanding its regional linguistic diversity. This lack of resources is not unique to Romanian, and many other languages around the world have similar challenges because they have lower visibility on the global linguistic stage. The VarDial workshop is one of the main drivers of the growing interest in language variety and dialect identification, by organizing multiple shared tasks each year.

Because deep learning frameworks have been successful in speech processing, researchers started to use such methods for low-resource languages. This has led to a growing need for resources on low-resource languages. If we look at dialect identification datasets across different languages, we can distinguish two types of resources: text-based datasets and speech-based datasets. Various languages have benefited from text-based resources that use written materials capturing linguistic variations, but the auditory dimension of dialects adds an intricate layer of complexity. Text data is valuable, but it might not fully capture the nuanced phonetic and prosodic characteristics that are pivotal for telling dialects apart. Audio datasets, in contrast to text datasets, give a more holistic representation, and they capture not only the lexical disparities but also the subtle intonations and accents that are inherent in speech.

As far as we know, RoDia is the first dataset to tackle spoken dialect identification in the Romanian landscape in accordance with historical, geographical and sociocultural factors, and it encourages research in this low-resource language. There are two text datasets that address Romanian dialect identification, MOROCO and MOROCO-Tweets, but they only cover two dialects: Romanian (equivalent to the Muntenesc dialect) and Moldavian (Moldovenesc). Our dataset is instead focused on speech and covers five Romanian dialects, as shown in Figure 1. The extra dialects, namely Ardelenesc, Bănăţean and Oltenesc, are very well characterized by phonetic differences that are captured only in speech. This is why MOROCO and MOROCO-Tweets only contain text samples from the other two dialects.

The number of audio datasets available in Romanian is rather low, which confirms that Romanian is indeed a low-resource language. The existing datasets with Romanian speech samples are mainly focused on automatic speech recognition, and they ignore the diversity of dialects in the region. Our dataset, on the other hand, is specifically designed to represent five distinct dialects spoken in Romania: Muntenesc (accepted as the official language of Romania), Ardelenesc, Moldovenesc, Oltenesc and Bănăţean.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Spoken dialect identification has emerged as a challenging task aiming at a fine-grained distinction between varieties of a certain language, with similar implications to spoken language identification [1,2,3]. Despite being a more delicate task, spoken dialect identification has received comparatively less attention, most of it devoted to dialect identification for widely spoken languages, such as English [4], Chinese [5], and Arabic [6,7,8]. Spoken dialect identification for low-resource languages, such as Swiss German [9,10] and Finnish [11], has remained relatively underexplored [12,1,11]. Different from prior studies, we focus on spoken language identification in Romanian, a low-resource language characterized by intricate dialectal variations within the country of Romania. Romanian, a Romance language with Latin roots, has a rich linguistic landscape shaped by historical, geographical, and sociocultural factors [13]. However, despite its linguistic complexity, Romanian remains a low-resource language, with limited studies dedicated to understanding its regional linguistic diversity. This scarcity of resources is not unique to Romanian, as numerous other languages around the world face similar challenges due to their lower visibility on the global linguistic stage [12,1,11]. Notably, the VarDial workshop is one of the main drivers of the growing interest in language variety and dialect identification, through the organization of multiple shared tasks each year [14,15,16,17].

Due to the success of deep learning frameworks in speech processing [18], researchers started to employ such methods for low-resource languages [19,20]. This has led to a growing need for resources on low-resource languages. Considering dialect identification datasets across different languages, we can distinguish between two types of resources: text-based datasets [21,22,23,24,25] and speech-based datasets [6,7,8,9,10,11]. While various languages have benefited from text-based resources that leverage written materials capturing linguistic variations, the auditory dimension of dialects adds an intricate layer of complexity. Text data, although valuable, might not fully capture the nuanced phonetic and prosodic characteristics that are pivotal in dialect differentiation. In contrast to text datasets, audio datasets [6,7,8,9,10] offer a more holistic representation, capturing not only the lexical disparities, but also the subtle intonations and accents inherent in speech.

To the best of our knowledge, RoDia is the first dataset to tackle spoken dialect identification in the Romanian landscape in accordance with historical, geographical, and sociocultural factors, encouraging research in this low-resource language. Although two text datasets address Romanian dialect identification, MOROCO [22] and MOROCO-Tweets [25], these cover only two dialects: Romanian (equivalent to the Muntenesc dialect) and Moldavian (Moldovenesc). In contrast, our dataset is focused on speech and covers five Romanian dialects, as shown in Figure 1. We note that the extra dialects, namely Ardelenesc, Bănăţean, and Oltenesc, are very well characterized by phonetic differences captured only in speech. This explains why MOROCO [22] and MOROCO-Tweets [25] only contain text samples from the other two dialects.

The number of audio datasets available in Romanian is rather low [26,27], confirming that Romanian is indeed a low-resource language. We note that existing datasets comprising Romanian speech samples are mainly focused on automatic speech recognition, ignoring the diversity of dialects within the region. In contrast, our dataset is specifically designed to represent five distinct dialects spoken in Romania: Muntenesc (accepted as the official language of Romania), Ardelenesc, Moldovenesc, Oltenesc, and Bănăţean.
